Exilée et enceinte: les affres de Marie*: Exiled and Pregnant: Marie*'s Ordeal Searching for Housing
Lorsqu'elle atterrit à Montréal, Marie*: When she lands in Montréal, Marie* has $200 in her pocket and two priorities: to check on the state of her pregnancy and to get to her temporary accommodation.
Marie* livre son parcours pour mettre de: Marie* shares her journey to highlight the work of the community organizations that helped her as a pregnant asylum seeker. Illustration: Sonia Ekiyor-Katimi
Alors qu’elle pense être en sécurité apr: Just when she thinks she is safe after fleeing Guinea-Conakry, Marie (a pseudonym) faces a new series of problems in Montréal. Portrait of a political activist seeking asylum in Canada.
Enceinte de huit mois, elle arrive en re: Eight months pregnant, she arrives late to our meeting. It is a cold, rainy day, the kind April can deliver in Montréal. “I had to beg the bus driver to let me on because there was no money left on my Opus card,” says the 21-year-old mother. She meets me at the offices of Femmes du monde à Côte-des-Neiges, an organization that has supported her since she arrived in the city.
En 2023, 111 demandeurs d’asile <l1>en p: In 2023, 111 asylum seekers <l1>from Guinea</l1> were accepted in Canada. A tiny diaspora from a country in the midst of major political turmoil.
Lorsqu’elle atterrit à l’aéroport Pierre: When she lands at Pierre-Elliott-Trudeau airport in Montréal, Marie has only $200 in her pocket and two priorities: to go to the hospital to check on the health of her unborn child and to join the friend who is supposed to host her temporarily. It is the start of a series of disappointments.
D’abord, on refuse de l’admettre à l’hôp: First, she is refused admission at the hospital, even though she is worried after a flight of more than eight hours while almost eight months pregnant.
« Au lieu de me prendre d’abord, de voir: “Instead of seeing me first, checking whether I had any problems, and talking to me about money afterward, they asked me for my status,” she says indignantly. “When I said I had a student visa, that I had no health insurance card and that I was pregnant, they told me to come back with proper documents.” Anxious, she leaves the hospital in tears, telling herself she would have been willing to go into debt just to get an ultrasound and make sure her baby was healthy.
Marie appartient alors à la catégorie «: Marie then falls into the category of “Migrant without health insurance” (MSAM), about which <l1>bioethics researcher Annie Liv</l1> says: “When they are pregnant, some MSAM women forgo obstetric care because they cannot afford medical fees that can range between $8,934 and $17,280.”
C’est après cet épisode où on lui a refu: It is after this episode, in which she was denied access to health care, that Marie decides to file an asylum claim, because she fears for her safety in Guinea. An agent from the Service d’Interprète d’Aide et de Référence aux Immigrants (SIARI) helps her fill out her claim, and she then receives an acknowledgment of receipt, the essential document for obtaining health care. “It was like arriving in paradise!” she exclaims.
Mais une autre désillusion attendait Mar: But another disappointment awaited Marie: the welcome at her friend’s place. “Some people aren’t kind,” she lets slip. She sleeps on the floor at this woman’s home while pregnant, and eats leftovers for a few weeks.
« J’apprends ensuite qu’on peut obtenir: “Then I learned that you can get housing through PRAIDA [Programme régional d’accueil et d’intégration des demandeurs d’asile, Editor’s note] and the YMCA, but only if you claim asylum at the airport,” an absurdity she cannot explain.
« C’est le même processus, mais pourquoi: “It’s the same process, so why this distinction? I was able to change my status from student to asylum seeker thanks to meeting SIARI.” “The tears flowed right there because I was completely desperate.”
Contacté par La Converse, le PRAIDA affi: Contacted by La Converse, PRAIDA says there is no distinction among asylum seekers based on where they file their claim.
S’il ne commente aucun cas particulier,: While he does not comment on any individual case, the spokesperson for the organization that welcomes asylum seekers in Montréal is surprised by this situation, because “access to PRAIDA’s temporary housing is granted following a rigorous assessment by a social worker.”
Quatre critères donnent accès à l’héberg: Four criteria give access to temporary housing: you must be an asylum seeker in due form, meaning you have an acknowledgment of receipt; be “newly arrived”; have no financial resources; and have no network that can take you in.
Encore au lycée – l’équivalent du second: While still in lycée, the equivalent of high school in Quebec, Marie gets involved in politics early. She joins the ranks of the <l1>Union des forces démocratiques de Guinée (UFDG)</l1> and gives speeches to mobilize the base.
« Dans ma communauté, c’était mal vu qu’: “In my community, it was frowned upon for a girl from the Mandinka ethnic group to be part of the UFDG,” she explains, still passionate about politics. “It was ethnic. There was segregation in my circle.” Even though members of the Mandinka ethnic group are also part of the UFDG, it is possible that Marie faced difficulties in her community or her family.
Elle explique avoir reçu de nombreuses i: She says she received many insults from members of the Mandinka community she belongs to, who blamed her for joining a political party associated with the Fulani people. “In the street, they threw stones at us because we wore shirts with the UFDG logo. It was frowned upon for me to mix with the Fulani. But I saw what was right,” she recounts.
Dans un climat politique tendu où le par: In a tense political climate in which the ruling party wins a third term, Marie decides to leave the country, and quickly.
« Nous étions comme des fourmis : les me: “We were like ants: the members of the new government wanted to crush us. When they knew you were UFDG, they knew you were against the regime, categorically against the state. And when your Mandinka community knows you’re on the side of the Fulani, it goes badly,” she explains.
Le coup d’État de septembre 2021 mené pa: The September 2021 military coup that overthrew the Rassemblement du peuple de Guinée (RPG) temporarily changes things. Colonel Mamadi Doumbouya is at the head of the operation. “When they took power, all the opponents were happy,” she says softly. She then gives up the idea of fleeing her country. But soon, the colonel changes course.
« C’était catastrophique. <l1>Il s’est m: “It was catastrophic. <l1>He started hunting down all the members of all the political parties existing in Guinea</l1>. Young, old, it didn’t matter, they would take you and throw you in prison,” says the young woman. This situation forces her to rethink her plans.
<strong>Un choix déchirant entre mariage: A heartbreaking choice between marriage and family
Entre-temps, Marie rencontre son futur é: In the meantime, Marie meets her future husband at an Islamic conference. “It was during the month of Ramadan, and we got along well, so we exchanged contact information,” she says, smiling.
Marie, qui vit alors avec ses parents ch: Marie, who is then living with her parents at her uncle’s house, asks him for financial help to apply for a student visa and go to Canada. He is the one with the money, and he owns the house. She decides to continue her studies in Quebec by joining the Campus Canada program, and in doing so to flee the unstable political situation in her country. She knows that her political involvement with the UFDG <l1>makes her a potential target</l1>.
Son fiancé vient demander sa main à ses: Her fiancé comes to ask her parents for her hand. “My parents turned him away, especially my uncle, who was financing my application, and why? Because he wanted me to marry his eldest son,” she says angrily. “When my husband came to ask for my hand, my uncle told me to choose between my trip and my husband. But I loved him and he loved me too. They kicked me out of the house, and I left and went to where my husband was staying.”
L’attente de Marie prend bientôt fin, ma: Marie’s wait soon comes to an end, but it is only one stage. “I gave birth to my first baby in Guinea. After a month, the visa arrived.” It will still take her two years to save the funds needed to buy a plane ticket.
« Mon mari s’est battu pour amasser l’ar: “My husband fought to raise the money. He couldn’t work openly for the regime in power, because his wife was wanted,” she says, moved, thinking back on her husband who worked tirelessly.
Lorsqu’elle arrive à Montréal, le chemin: When she arrives in Montréal, Marie’s ordeal to find housing begins. She believes that without SIARI’s support, she would be on the street today, experiencing homelessness.
Après un refus du PRAIDA, une intervenan: After PRAIDA turns her down, a SIARI caseworker calls every emergency shelter that takes in women, relentlessly. She finds a temporary solution at Le Chaînon. This centre normally houses women who are victims of domestic violence, but a bed is free in a dormitory. While she looks for something else, Marie catches her breath, relieved. She narrowly avoids the street, because the friend who had been hosting her temporarily gave her an ultimatum to leave and find her own housing.
« Je ne suis pas habituée à la fraîcheur: “I’m not used to the cold, and I was wondering whether I’d be able to sleep outside in March,” she recalls, tears in her eyes. Then good news arrives: another organization, Passages, has a free bed in a room. Once again, this emergency housing eases her path.
« Là-bas, j’étais dans une chambre avec: “There, I was in a room with two beds and they also provided meals. I was so happy to have a roof over my head, my own little bed,” says Marie, a smile on her lips.
Mais les réjouissances sont de courte du: But the celebration is short-lived: “They told me I absolutely had to find more permanent housing, because if I gave birth without a home, the DPJ [youth protection services] could take my child away. I was completely shaken. It was not okay at all.”
Tenaillée par la crainte, Marie ne sait: Gripped by fear, Marie does not know, however, that an entire team is working to find her a more permanent solution.
« Si je commence à parler du rôle du SIA: “If I start talking about SIARI’s role, I’m going to start crying,” she says, moved. “I don’t want to say they only help with material things, but they were there with me. The day I claimed asylum, they lifted my spirits by telling me they would find solutions, and indeed, they found solutions.”
Une travailleuse sociale de Femmes du mo: A social worker at Femmes du monde à Côte-des-Neiges tells Marie that she and her team worked tirelessly to find her emergency housing and to get her a gift card to buy food at a supermarket. It is a fine example of the work that community organizations, buckling under requests and needs, do behind the scenes and in synergy. “We were behind the scenes, talking and looking for housing. Marie would come late and leave late,” says Christina Pierre, community organizer at Femmes du monde.
Cette solution exclut le risque, pour Ma: This solution rules out the risk, for Marie, of having her baby taken away, a baby she expects any day now.
« Tout le monde m’a bien accueillie ! Le: “Everyone welcomed me warmly! My spirits are good now, because as for the pregnancy, I’m being followed by La Maison Bleue,” she says, a big smile in her voice.
D’ici à ce que son mari et sa fille aîné: Until her husband and eldest daughter join her in Montréal, Marie says she will have the strength to keep studying once her two children are older. “I dream of studying economics and working for the World Bank,” she says, adding that she wants to make her country of origin shine.
En attendant, elle souhaite s’ouvrir sur: In the meantime, she wants to open up about her story so that things change and so that pregnant women who claim asylum are better informed about what awaits them when they arrive in Canada. “This is really not the end of your troubles, and it could be harder than you think,” she says, before adding that the help offered by community organizations is a lifeline.
« Ce qu’ils font, vraiment, ça mérite de: “What they do, really, deserves medals,” Marie exclaims, laughing.
